title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: PRIVATE COMPANIES IN SPACE SECTOR
body_text:
As per the DPIIT Start-up India Portal , around 440 space technology startups are registered in India. IN-SPACe has granted 113 authorisations to 52 Non-Government Entities (NGEs) to carry out various space activities, out of which 18 are start-ups. The details are as under:
Agnikul Cosmos Pvt Ltd, Akshath Aerospace Private Limited, Azista BST, Bellatrix Aerospace Pvt Ltd, Cosmoserv Space India Private Limited, Dhruva Space Private Limited, Digantara Research and Technologies Pvt. Ltd GalaxEye Space Solutions Private Limited, HEX20Labs India Pvt ltd., Inorbit Space Telecommunications Private Limited, Manastu Space Technologies Private Limited, NSpace Tech India Private Limited, OrbitAID Aerospace Private Limited, PierSight Space Private Limited, PixxelSpace India Private Limited, Skyroot Aerospace Private Limited, Space Kidz India, TakeMe2Space Technologies Pvt. Ltd,
The applications for usage and access to ISRO infrastructure (including the launch pads at ISRO's Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota) are processed as per the standard SOP based on the application received by IN-SPACe on its Digital Platform and the readiness aspects are reviewed by an Expert Committee of IN-SPACe.
The total number of commercial rockets are proposed to be launched by Indian private companies over the next two years are as under:
FY 26-27: 02 nos.
FY 27-28: The Launch manifest is yet to be approved by IN-SPACe. It is expected that more than 06 nos. of launches may be undertaken by Indian Private Companies.
This information was given by Union Minister of State for Prime Minister’s office and
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, in a written reply in the Rajya Sabha today
****
NKR/AK/NM

enrichment.summary: In a written Rajya Sabha reply, Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh stated that around 440 space technology startups are registered under the DPIIT Start-up India Portal, and IN-SPACe has granted 113 authorisations to 52 Non-Government Entities (NGEs), including 18 startups, for various space activities. He also disclosed that private Indian companies are expected to launch 2 commercial rockets in FY 2026-27 and more than 6 in FY 2027-28, subject to IN-SPACe's launch manifest approval.
enrichment.context:
IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre) was established in 2020 as an autonomous nodal agency under the Department of Space to promote, hand-hold, authorise, and regulate private sector participation in space activities, marking a major shift from ISRO's monopoly to a liberalized 'Space Reforms' regime announced in June 2020. This is part of India's broader push to open the space sector to private players, enable access to ISRO facilities like the Satish Dhawan Space Centre for launches, and boost the domestic space economy, which the government aims to grow significantly (targeting a multi-fold increase in India's share of the global space economy by 2033 under the Indian Space Policy 2023).

Companies like Skyroot Aerospace (which launched India's first privately developed rocket, Vikram-S, in 2022), Agnikul Cosmos (developer of 3D-printed rocket engines), Pixxel (Earth observation satellites), and Dhruva Space are frontrunners in this ecosystem. The growth in NGE authorisations and startup registrations reflects increasing private investment, ease-of-doing-business reforms, and the government's intent to position India as a competitive player in the global commercial space launch and satellite services market, alongside players like SpaceX and Rocket Lab.

prelims_questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding IN-SPACe:
1. It is an autonomous nodal agency under the Department of Space.
2. It authorises Non-Government Entities (NGEs) to carry out space activities.
3. It was established as part of the Indian Space Policy, 2023.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: IN-SPACe is an autonomous nodal agency under the Department of Space that authorises and regulates NGEs for space activities. It was established in 2020 as part of the space sector reforms, prior to and independent of the Indian Space Policy 2023, so statement 3 is incorrect.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following Indian private companies is known for developing a 3D-printed rocket engine and launch vehicle?
prelims_questions.explanation: Agnikul Cosmos is notable for its 3D-printed rocket engine technology used in its Agnibaan launch vehicle, distinguishing it among Indian private space startups.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of opening up India's space sector to private participation. Examine the role of IN-SPACe in facilitating this transition and the challenges that remain.

India's space economy is poised for significant growth with increasing private sector involvement. Analyze the policy and infrastructural reforms needed to sustain this growth and enhance India's competitiveness in the global commercial space launch market.
